Battle of Salamis. In 480 BC, in the narrow straits around the island of Salamis near Athens, the allied Greek fleet delivered a decisive blow to the vastly larger Persian navy. The victory ended Persian hopes of conquering Greece and established naval dominance as the foundation of Athenian power.

The Athenian admiral Themistocles commanded the Greek forces and had devised a brilliant strategy. He deliberately lured the Persian fleet into the confined waters of the straits, where numbers meant far less than maneuverability and ship handling.

The Greek alliance fielded around 370 triremes, while the Persians brought over 1,200 vessels. In open sea, this overwhelming advantage would have decided the day. But the narrow straits prevented the Persians from using their numbers. Greek ships were faster and better coordinated, and in those close quarters they could operate at peak efficiency while the Persian fleet became a liability to itself.

The casualties told the tale. The Persians lost approximately 200 to 300 ships. The Greeks lost only around 40. Xerxes I watched the battle from the shore and reportedly despaired at the sight of his navy being destroyed. He began planning his retreat to Asia.

The victory secured Greek independence and transformed Athens into the preeminent naval power of the eastern Mediterranean. Themistocles, the brilliant admiral whose strategy turned numbers into weakness, had changed history. Xerxes, who had invaded Greece with what seemed like infinite power, saw his ambitions shattered. The Persian Wars themselves were essentially concluded by Salamis, though the land battle at Plataea would follow to seal the outcome.
